title: Plutarch and Varro: Egyptian animals and human-shaped gods are mystical vessels, not crude bodies of deity
source_text: XX. Et quidem quod attinet animalium figuras, aut etiam ipsa animalia viva ab Aegyptiis culta, Plutarchus idem, tractatu de Iside & Osiride, prolixe docet varias numinis virtutes, atque beneficia, iis fuisse mystice & symbolice adumbrata. Apud Augustinum vero de Civitate Dei Varro testatur, Antiquos, qui Deorum simulachra hominis specie fecerunt, hoc videri secutos, quod mortalium animus qui est in corpore humano, simillimus sit immortalis animi: tanquam si vasa ponerentur causa notandorum Deorum, & in Liberi aede Oenophorum sisteretur quod significaret vitem, per id quod continet, id quod continetur: ita per simulachrum quod formam haberet humanam, significari animam rationalem, eo quod velut vase, natura ista soleat contineri, cujus naturae volunt Deum esse, vel Deos. lib. 7. cap. 5.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed as concerns the figures of animals, or even the living animals themselves cultivated by the Egyptians, the same Plutarch, in the treatise on Isis and Osiris, teaches at length that various virtues and benefits of the divinity were mystically and symbolically shadowed by them. But in Augustine On the City of God Varro testifies that the Ancients, who made the simulacra of the Gods in the species of a man, seem to have followed this, that the mind of mortals which is in the human body is most like the immortal mind: as if vessels were set for the sake of noting the Gods, and in the temple of Liber an Oenophorum were set which would signify the vine, through that which contains, that which is contained: so through a simulacrum which had human form, a rational soul is signified, because as in a vessel that nature is accustomed to be contained, of which nature they will that God, or the Gods, be. book 7, chapter 5.
pass_b_english: Plutarch’s Isis treatise reads Egyptian animal cult as mystical symbolism of divine virtues.
Varro (via Augustine, Civ. 7.5): human-shaped gods are vessels signifying rational soul— Liber’s wine-jar for the vine.

choices.why: Plutarch’s tract on symbolic animal cult.
